title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the Eighth Batch of Guiding Cases
ruling_gist_en:
1. Motor vehicle drivers who, for the purposes of competition, thrill-seeking, venting anger, or other motives, weave through traffic or rapidly chase other vehicles on the road, constitute "chase racing" as stipulated in Article 133-1 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China.

2. Although chase racing may not cause casualties or property damage, if, taking into comprehensive consideration acts that seriously violate road traffic safety laws such as exceeding the speed limit, running red lights, forcibly overtaking, resisting traffic law enforcement, etc., it is sufficient to threaten the life or property of others, then it constitutes a "flagrant circumstance" under the crime of dangerous driving.
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Issuing the Eighth Batch of Guiding Cases

Fa [2014] No. 327

To: High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; and the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

Upon deliberation and decision by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, the following six cases (Guiding Cases No. 32-37), including the case of Zhang and Jin on dangerous driving, are hereby issued as the eighth batch of guiding cases for reference in adjudicating similar cases.

December 18, 2014

Guiding Case No. 32

Zhang and Jin v. Dangerous Driving

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court on December 18, 2014)

Keywords: Criminal; Crime of dangerous driving; Drag racing; Flagrant circumstances

Ruling Gist

1. Where a motor vehicle driver, out of motives such as competition, pursuit of excitement, confrontation, or other motives, drives in a zigzag manner on the road or rapidly chases other vehicles, such conduct falls under "drag racing" as provided in Article 133-1 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China.

2. Although drag racing may not cause personal injury or property damage, if, when considered comprehensively, the conduct involves serious violations of road traffic safety laws, such as speeding, running red lights, forced overtaking, or resisting traffic enforcement, and is sufficient to threaten the life or property safety of others, it constitutes a "flagrant circumstance" under the crime of dangerous driving.

Relevant Legal Provision

Article 133-1 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

At approximately 20:20 on February 3, 2012, the defendants Zhang and Jin agreed to ride motorcycles to enjoy the thrill of high-powered motorcycles, and agreed that "the intersection of Lujiabang Road and Henan South Road is the destination, and whoever arrives first will wait for the other." Subsequently, Zhang drove an unlicensed modified Honda high-power two-wheel motorcycle, and Jin drove a modified Yamaha high-power two-wheel motorcycle with a counterfeit license plate. They started from No. 99 Leyuan Road, Pudong New Area, Shanghai, drove to the intersection of Yanggao Road and Jufeng Road, made a U-turn, drove south along Yanggao Road, crossed Nanpu Bridge, went down the bridge at Lujiabang Road, then proceeded along Henan South Road through Fuxing East Road Tunnel, and finally along Zhangyang Road back to Zhang's residence. The entire journey was 28.5 kilometers, passing multiple bus stops, residential communities, schools, and large supermarkets. During the drive, the two defendants repeatedly changed lanes, wove through dense traffic, ran multiple red lights, and drove at significantly excessive speeds. When they arrived at the intersection of Lujiabang Road and Henan South Road, Zhang and Jin encountered police officers conducting checks. They then drove away along Henan South Road through Fuxing East Road Tunnel and Zhangyang Road to escape. Among other locations, at the Yanggao South Road Pujian Road interchange (speed limit 60 km/h), Zhang's speed was 115 km/h and Jin's speed was 98 km/h; on the deck of Nanpu Bridge (speed limit 60 km/h), Zhang's speed was 108 km/h and Jin's speed was 108 km/h; on the off-ramp of Nanpu Bridge at Lujiabang Road (speed limit 40 km/h), Zhang's speed was over 59 km/h and Jin's speed was over 68 km/h; in Fuxing East Road Tunnel (speed limit 60 km/h), Zhang's speed was 102 km/h and Jin's speed was 99 km/h.

At approximately 21:00 on February 5, 2012, defendant Zhang was arrested and, upon arrest, truthfully confessed to the above facts and provided the police with defendant Jin's mobile phone number. After receiving a telephone notice from the police, defendant Jin voluntarily surrendered at approximately 21:00 on February 6, 2012, and truthfully confessed to the above facts.

Judgment

The Pudong New Area People's Court of Shanghai, on January 21, 2013, rendered criminal judgment (2012) Pu Xing Chu Zi No. 4245: Defendant Zhang was convicted of the crime of dangerous driving and sentenced to criminal detention for four months, with a four-month suspension of execution, and a fine of RMB 4,000; defendant Jin was convicted of the crime of dangerous driving and sentenced to criminal detention for three months, with a three-month suspension of execution, and a fine of RMB 3,000. After the judgment was announced, neither defendant appealed, and the judgment has become legally effective.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: According to Article 133-1, paragraph 1, of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China, "drag racing a motor vehicle on a road under flagrant circumstances" constitutes the crime of dangerous driving. The term "drag racing" as used in the Criminal Law generally refers to conduct where two or more persons, out of motives such as competition, pursuit of excitement, confrontation, or other motives, respectively drive motor vehicles, violate road traffic safety regulations, and rapidly chase each other on the road. In this case, from the subjective driving mentality, after being brought to justice, the two defendants Zhang and Jin successively stated that "they wanted to find some pleasure and excitement," "weaving through traffic and overtaking gave them psychological satisfaction," and when facing red lights, "it felt uncomfortable to brake; they overtook every car in front, and if there was a car ahead, they would change lanes, weave, and then overtake." The above statements of the two defendants corroborated with relevant audio-visual materials, reflecting their competitive mentality of pursuing excitement and showing off driving skills. From the objective conduct, the two defendants drove modified high-power motorcycles exceeding standards, and to pursue speed, they repeatedly engaged in serious violations such as arbitrarily changing lanes, running red lights, and grossly exceeding speed limits. From the driving route, the two defendants jointly started from No. 99 Leyuan Road in Pudong New Area and went to the intersection of Lujiabang Road and Henan South Road to pick up someone, setting a starting point and destination for competitive driving. In summary, it can be determined that the conduct of the two defendants constituted "drag racing" under the crime of dangerous driving.

Regarding whether the conduct of the defendants in this case constituted "flagrant circumstances," it should be comprehensively analyzed from the specific manifestations, degree of harm, and consequences of the drag racing conduct, and whether the degree of threat to road traffic order and the life and property safety of an unspecified number of persons was "flagrant." In this case, although the drag racing conduct of the two defendants did not cause personal injury or property damage, analysis of the following circumstances shows that it constituted "flagrant circumstances" under the crime of dangerous driving: First, from the type of vehicle driven, the two defendants drove unlicensed and counterfeit-licensed modified high-power motorcycles; second, from the driving speed, the overall driving speed was very fast, and at multiple sections, the speed exceeded the limit by over 50%; third, from the driving method, they repeatedly changed lanes, wove in front of other vehicles, and ran multiple red lights; fourth, from their attitude toward law enforcement, the two defendants drove away when police officers were checking; fifth, from the road sections traveled, the roads they passed, including Yanggao Road, Zhangyang Road, Nanpu Bridge, and Fuxing East Road Tunnel, were all urban main roads, and along the way there were multiple schools, bus and subway stations, residential communities, large supermarkets, and other locations, with heavy traffic and a long driving distance. Under the stimulating mentality of high-speed driving and the tense mentality of evading police checks, it was highly likely to cause serious major traffic accidents. The above conduct created a certain danger to public traffic safety and was sufficient to threaten the life and property safety of others. Therefore, it can be determined that the drag racing conduct of the two defendants constituted "flagrant circumstances" under the crime of dangerous driving.

After being brought to justice, defendant Zhang truthfully confessed to the crimes he committed and could be given a lighter punishment according to law. Defendant Jin voluntarily surrendered and could also be given a lighter punishment according to law. Given that both defendants recognized the illegality and social harmfulness of their conduct during the trial, guaranteed not to engage in dangerous driving again, and repeatedly expressed remorse and repentance, and that their conduct had not yet caused harm to others' persons or property, the above judgment was rendered according to law.

Guiding Case No. 33

Cargill International SA v. Fujian Jinshi Oil Co., Ltd. et al. — Dispute over Confirmation of Contract Invalidity

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court on December 18, 2014)

Keywords: Civil; Confirmation of contract invalidity; Malicious collusion; Return of property

Ruling Gist

1. Where a debtor transfers its principal assets to its affiliated company at a clearly unreasonably low price, and the affiliated company, knowing that the debtor is in debt, does not actually pay the consideration, it may be determined that the debtor and its affiliated company have maliciously colluded to harm the interests of the creditor, and the property transfer contract relating thereto shall be deemed invalid.

2. Article 59 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China applies to circumstances where a third party is the owner of the property. Where a creditor holds a general claim against the debtor, according to Article 58 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, the property obtained under the invalid contract shall be ordered to be returned to the original property owner, and the property obtained by the debtor's affiliated company from the debtor under a contract of "malicious collusion harming third party interests" shall not be directly ordered to be returned to the creditor pursuant to Article 59.

Relevant Legal Provisions

1. Article 52, item (2) of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

2. Articles 58 and 59 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China

Basic Facts

Cargill International SA (hereinafter "Cargill") had a commercial cooperative relationship with Fujian Jinshi Oil Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Fujian Jinshi") and Dalian Jinshi Oil Co., Ltd., Shenyang Jinshi Bean Industry Co., Ltd., Sichuan Jinshi Oil Meal Co., Ltd., Beijing Kema Meijia Grain and Oil Co., Ltd., and Yifeng Hong Kong Co., Ltd. (these six companies are collectively referred to as "Jinshi Group"). A dispute arose between Cargill and Jinshi Group over the purchase and sale of soybeans. During the arbitration proceedings before the International Federation of Oils, Seeds and Fats Associations (FOSFA), on June 26, 2005, the parties reached a Settlement Agreement, providing that Jinshi Group would repay the debt in installments over five years and would mortgage all assets of Fujian Jinshi, a subsidiary of Jinshi Group, including land use rights, buildings and fixtures, all equipment, and other property, to Cargill as security for the debt repayment. On October 10, 2005, FOSFA issued Arbitration Award No. 3929 based on the Settlement Agreement, confirming that Jinshi Group should pay Cargill USD 13.37 million. In May 2006, because Jinshi Group failed to perform the arbitration award and Fujian Jinshi did not cooperate in the asset mortgage, Cargill applied to the Xiamen Intermediate People's Court of Fujian Province for recognition and enforcement of Arbitration Award No. 3929. On June 26, 2007, after review, the Xiamen Intermediate People's Court ruled to recognize and enforce the legal effect of the arbitration award. After the ruling became effective, Cargill applied for compulsory enforcement.

On May 8, 2006, Fujian Jinshi and Fujian Tianyuan Bio-Protein Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Tianyuan") entered into a Contract for the Sale of State-Owned Land Use Rights and Assets, providing that Fujian Jinshi would sell all its fixed assets, including state-owned land use rights, factory buildings, office buildings, and oil production equipment, to Tianyuan at a price of RMB 25.69 million (unless otherwise specified, all amounts are in RMB), of which the state-owned land use rights were valued at RMB 4.64 million, and the buildings and equipment were valued at RMB 21.05 million, with full payment due within 30 days after the contract took effect. Wang Xiaoqi and Liu Feng signed the contract as the legal representatives of Fujian Jinshi and Tianyuan, respectively. Fujian Jinshi had acquired the 32,138 square meters of state-owned land use rights involved in the case on December 31, 2001, at a price of RMB 4.821 million. On May 10, 2006, Fujian Jinshi and Tianyuan conducted a handover of the subject matter under the sale contract. On June 15 of the same year, Tianyuan transferred RMB 25 million from its account at the Agricultural Bank of China, Zhangzhou Branch, to Fujian Jinshi's account at the same bank. On the same day, Fujian Jinshi transferred two sums of RMB 13 million and RMB 12 million from that account to the account of Dalian Jinshi Oil Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of Jinshi Group, designated as current account payments. On June 19, 2006, Tianyuan obtained the aforementioned state-owned land use right certificate.

On February 21, 2008, Tianyuan and Zhangzhou Development Zone Huifengyuan Trading Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Huifengyuan") entered into a Sale Contract, providing that Huifengyuan would purchase the aforementioned land use rights, above-ground buildings, and equipment at a total price of RMB 26.69 million, of which the land price was RMB 6.03 million, the building price was RMB 3.34 million, and the equipment price was RMB 17.32 million. Huifengyuan obtained the aforementioned state-owned land use right certificate in March 2008. Huifengyuan only paid Tianyuan RMB 5.69 million on April 7, 2008, and did not pay the remaining price thereafter.

The direct or indirect controllers of Tianyuan, Fujian Jinshi, Dalian Jinshi Oil Co., Ltd., and other companies under Jinshi Group were Wang Zhengliang, Wang Xiaoli, Wang Xiaoqi, and Liu Feng. Wang Zhengliang is the father of Wang Xiaoqi and Wang Xiaoli, and Liu Feng is the husband of Wang Xiaoqi. On October 15, 2009, China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Cofco Oils") acquired 80% of the equity of Tianyuan. On January 15, 2010, Tianyuan changed its name to Cofco Oils (Fujian) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Cofco Fujian").

Huifengyuan was established on February 19, 2008, with original shareholders Song Mingquan and Yang Shuli. On September 16, 2009, Cofco Oils entered into an Equity Transfer Agreement with Song Mingquan and Yang Shuli, providing that Cofco Oils would purchase 80% of the equity of Huifengyuan. On the same day, Cofco Oils (Party A), Huifengyuan (Party B), Song Mingquan and Yang Shuli (Party C), and Shenyang Jindou Food Co., Ltd. (Party D) entered into an Equity Pledge Agreement, providing that Party C would pledge its 20% equity in Huifengyuan to Party A as security for the performance of the "contractual obligations" of Parties B, C, and D; "contractual obligations" referred to all responsibilities and obligations of Parties B and C under the Equity Transfer Agreement and the Equity Pledge Agreement arising from the "Red Bean Incident"; the "Red Bean Incident" referred to a series of lawsuits and arbitration disputes involving Jinshi Group triggered by the admixture of red beans in imported soybeans between Cargill and Jinshi Group, as well as a series of related lawsuits and arbitration disputes involving Huifengyuan. It was also agreed that the "contractual obligations" of Parties B and C would be deemed fully performed on the date when the following circumstances concurrently occurred: 1. all trial and enforcement proceedings of any lawsuits or arbitration cases arising from the "Red Bean Incident" were fully concluded, and Party B had not suffered property losses; 2. any right of revocation that Cargill might have against the contracts involving Party B was extinguished due to the expiration of the maximum statutory period (five years). On November 18, 2009, Cofco Oils acquired 80% of the equity of Huifengyuan. Huifengyuan did not engage in actual business after its establishment.

Because Fujian Jinshi had no executable property, rendering enforcement impossible, Cargill filed a lawsuit with the Fujian High People's Court, requesting: first, confirmation that the Contract for the Sale of State-Owned Land Use Rights and Assets between Fujian Jinshi and Cofco Fujian was invalid; second, confirmation that the Sale Contract for state-owned land use rights and assets between Cofco Fujian and Huifengyuan was invalid; and third, an order that Huifengyuan and Cofco Fujian return the property obtained under the contracts to the property owner.

Judgment

The Fujian High People's Court, on October 23, 2011, rendered civil judgment (2007) Min Min Chu Zi No. 37, confirming that the Contract for the Sale of State-Owned Land Use Rights and Assets between Fujian Jinshi and Tianyuan (later renamed Cofco Fujian) and the Sale Contract between Tianyuan and Huifengyuan were invalid; ordering Huifengyuan to return to Fujian Jinshi the state-owned land use rights obtained under the said contracts within 30 days from the effective date of the judgment, and ordering Cofco Fujian to return to Fujian Jinshi the buildings and equipment obtained under the said contracts within 30 days from the effective date of the judgment. After the judgment was announced, Fujian Jinshi, Cofco Fujian, and Huifengyuan appealed. The Supreme People's Court, on August 22, 2012, rendered civil judgment (2012) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 1, dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held that: Because Cargill is registered in Switzerland, this case is a foreign-related case. The parties raised no objection to the application of the laws of the People's Republic of China to the trial of this case. This case originated from the creditor Cargill's claim that the sale contracts for land use rights, above-ground buildings, equipment, and other assets between the debtor Fujian Jinshi and its affiliated enterprise Tianyuan, and between Tianyuan and Huifengyuan, should be deemed invalid as they fell under Article 52, item (2) of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, i.e., "malicious collusion harming the interests of the state, the collective, or a third party," and Cargill demanded the return of the original property. The issues in dispute in this case were: whether the contracts concluded between Fujian Jinshi, Tianyuan (later renamed Cofco Fujian), and Huifengyuan constituted contracts of malicious collusion harming the interests of Cargill; and what were the legal consequences after the contracts involved in this case were deemed invalid.

I. Whether the contracts concluded between Fujian Jinshi, Tianyuan, and Huifengyuan constituted contracts of "malicious collusion harming the interests of a third party"

First, during the conclusion and performance of the Contract for the Sale of State-Owned Land Use Rights and Assets between Fujian Jinshi and Tianyuan, their actual controllers were related by family, and Liu Feng and Wang Xiaoqi, a married couple, signed the contract as legal representatives of the two companies, respectively. Therefore, it can be determined that during the signing and performance of the contract transferring Fujian Jinshi's state-owned land use rights, buildings, and equipment, Tianyuan was very aware of Fujian Jinshi's condition, and was aware of the fact that Jinshi Group, including Fujian Jinshi, had been confirmed by the arbitration award, due to the "Red Bean Incident," to owe Cargill a debt of USD 13.37 million.

Second, the Contract for the Sale of State-Owned Land Use Rights and Assets was concluded on May 8, 2006, and provided that the price for Tianyuan's purchase of Fujian Jinshi's assets was RMB 25.69 million, with the state-owned land use rights valued at RMB 4.64 million and the buildings and equipment valued at RMB 21.05 million, without being based on the appraisal report of a relevant accounting firm. The court of first instance, based on Fujian Jinshi's balance sheet as of May 31, 2006, which showed fixed assets at original cost of RMB 44,042,705.75 and fixed assets net of depreciation at RMB 32,354,833.70, and given that the Contract for the Sale of State-Owned Land Use Rights and Assets valued the buildings and equipment at only RMB 21.05 million, correctly determined that the price for the purchase of Fujian Jinshi's assets as agreed in the Contract for the Sale of State-Owned Land Use Rights and Assets was a clearly unreasonable low price. Knowing that the debtor Fujian Jinshi owed a huge debt to the creditor Cargill, Tianyuan purchased Fujian Jinshi's principal assets at a clearly unreasonably low price. This sufficiently proves that Tianyuan and Fujian Jinshi had subjective malice when concluding the Contract for the Sale of State-Owned Land Use Rights and Assets, constituting malicious collusion, and the performance of that contract was sufficient to harm the interests of the creditor Cargill.

Third, after the signing of the State-owned Land Use Right and Asset Sales Contract, although Tianyuan Company transferred RMB 25 million to Fujian Jinshi Company's account in the same bank, the transfer did not indicate the purpose of the funds. On the same day, Fujian Jinshi Company remitted the RMB 25 million in two installments to the account of its affiliated enterprise, Dalian Jinshi Oil Manufacturing Co., Ltd. Moreover, according to the financial statements of Fujian Jinshi Company and Tianyuan Company for that year, the RMB 25 million was not reflected as an entry or expenditure. Instead, it reflected that Tianyuan Company still owed Fujian Jinshi Company "other payables" of RMB 121,224,155.87. The court of first instance therefore reasonably found that Tianyuan Company did not actually pay the price to Fujian Jinshi Company under the State-owned Land Use Right and Asset Sales Contract.

Fourth, from the company registration records, the shareholder composition of Huifengyuan Company at the time of its establishment appeared unrelated to Fujian Jinshi Company. However, through the changes in Huifengyuan Company's equity, it could be seen that Huifengyuan Company, when signing the Sales Contract with Tianyuan Company, was aware of the source of the transferred assets and of Fujian Jinshi Company's debt to Cargill Company. The price stipulated in the Sales Contract was RMB 26.69 million, which was not significantly different from the price agreed upon when Tianyuan Company purchased the assets from Fujian Jinshi Company. Apart from having paid RMB 5.69 million to Tianyuan Company, Huifengyuan Company had not paid the remaining amount. The court of first instance therefore found that Huifengyuan Company and Tianyuan Company acted in malicious collusion when signing the Sales Contract, which was sufficient to harm the interests of creditor Cargill Company, and this finding was not improper.

In summary, the State-owned Land Use Right and Asset Sales Contract signed between Fujian Jinshi Company and Tianyuan Company, and the Sales Contract signed between Tianyuan Company and Huifengyuan Company, are contracts that involve malicious collusion and harm the interests of Cargill Company. Pursuant to Article 52, paragraph (2) of the Contract Law, both contracts shall be deemed invalid.

II. Legal Consequences After the Contracts Involved in This Case Are Found Invalid

For the handling of void contracts, the People's Court should generally, in accordance with Article 58 of the Contract Law, which provides: "After a contract is void or revoked, the property obtained under the contract shall be returned; if return is impossible or unnecessary, compensation shall be made in the form of appraisal. The party at fault shall compensate the other party for the losses suffered thereby; if both parties are at fault, each shall bear its own corresponding liability," order the party who obtained the property to return it. Both contracts involved in this case were found invalid, and the property involved in the two contracts is the same. Among this property, the state-owned land use right had been transferred from Fujian Jinshi Company to Tianyuan Company and then to Huifengyuan Company. In the absence of evidence that the building involved in this case had been transferred from Tianyuan Company to Huifengyuan Company, and that the equipment involved had been delivered from Tianyuan Company to Huifengyuan Company, the court of first instance directly ordered Huifengyuan Company, which obtained the state-owned land use right, and Tianyuan Company, which obtained the building and equipment, to return the property they had obtained to Fujian Jinshi Company, which was not improper.

Article 59 of the Contract Law provides: "Where the parties maliciously collude to harm the interests of the state, a collective, or a third party, the property obtained thereby shall be confiscated and turned over to the state or returned to the collective or the third party." This provision should be applied where the third party can be identified as the owner of the property. In this case, Cargill Company holds an ordinary claim against Fujian Jinshi Company. The property involved in this case is the property of Fujian Jinshi Company, not the property of Cargill Company. Therefore, only an order for the return of the disputed property to Fujian Jinshi Company can be made, and it cannot be directly ordered to be returned to Cargill Company.

Guiding Case No. 34

Li Xiaoling and Li Pengyu v. Xiamen Ocean Industry (Group) Co., Ltd. and Xiamen Ocean Industry Corporation — enforcement reconsideration case

(Adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on December 18, 2014)

Keywords: civil litigation; enforcement reconsideration; right successor; application for enforcement

Ruling Gist: Where the rights holder confirmed by an effective legal instrument lawfully transfers its claim before entering into the enforcement proceedings, the assignee of the claim, i.e., the right successor, may directly apply for enforcement as the applicant for enforcement without the need for the enforcement court to render a ruling on changing the applicant for enforcement.

Relevant Legal Provision: Article 236, paragraph 1, of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC

Basic Facts: In a loan contract dispute case of plaintiff Investments 2234 China Fund I B.V. (hereinafter referred to as 2234 Company) v. defendant Xiamen Ocean Industry (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Ocean Stock Company) and Xiamen Ocean Industry Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Ocean Industry Company), the Supreme People's Court rendered a final judgment on January 11, 2012, ordering: Ocean Industry Company shall repay the loan principal of RMB 22.74 million and corresponding interest to 2234 Company from the effective date of the judgment; 2234 Company enjoys a mortgage right over the land use right of No. 3 Fengchaoshan Road. Before this judgment was rendered, on June 8, 2011, 2234 Company transferred its claim for the principal of RMB 22.74 million against Ocean Stock Company and Ocean Industry Company to Li Xiaoling and Li Pengyu, and signed a Claim Assignment Agreement. On April 19, 2012, Li Xiaoling and Li Pengyu applied for enforcement to the Fujian High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as Fujian High Court) based on the above judgment and the Claim Assignment Agreement. On April 24, the Fujian High Court issued Enforcement Notice (2012) Min Zhi Xing Zi No. 8 to Ocean Stock Company and Ocean Industry Company. Ocean Stock Company objected to this enforcement notice, raising an enforcement objection with the Fujian High Court on the main grounds that directly changing the enforcement subject in the enforcement notice lacked legal basis, that the applicant for enforcement Li Pengyu was a civil servant, his assignment of the non-performing claim was invalid, and thus the claim assignment contract was invalid. During the review of the objection, the Fujian High Court found: Li Pengyu was a state civil servant. He himself stated that he had not actually contributed capital in the claim assignment and had already withdrawn from the assigned claim shares in September 2011.

The Fujian High Court held: 1. Regarding the validity of the claim assignment contract. According to paragraph 6 of the Supreme People's Court's Minutes of the Symposium on the Trial of Cases Involving the Transfer of Financial Non-performing Claims (hereinafter referred to as the Minutes), which provides that it is invalid where the transferee of a non-performing claim transferred by a financial asset management company is "a state civil servant or an employee of a financial regulatory institution," and Article 53, item (14) of the Civil Servant Law of the PRC which expressly prohibits state civil servants from engaging in or participating in for-profit activities, etc., Li Pengyu, as one of the transferees of the claim, was a state civil servant and his purchase of the claim was restricted by his status eligibility. Li Pengyu claimed that he had withdrawn from the assigned claim shares. The enforcement case accepted by this court still listed Li Pengyu as an applicant for enforcement without review, which was clearly improper. 2. Regarding the issue of directly changing the enforcement subject in the enforcement notice. The Supreme People's Court's (2009) Zhi Ta Zi No. 1 Reply on the Request for Instructions on Whether the People's Court Can Rule to Change the Applicant for Enforcement in Cases of Multiple Transfers of Non-performing Claims Determined by Judgment (hereinafter referred to as Reply No. 1) opined: "The Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Several Issues Concerning the Enforcement Work of the People's Court (for Trial Implementation) (hereinafter referred to as the Enforcement Provisions) has already clarified the qualifications of applicants for enforcement. Article 18, paragraph 1 thereof provides: 'The People's Court shall meet the following conditions for accepting enforcement cases: ... (2) The applicant for enforcement is the rights holder confirmed by the effective legal instrument or its successor or right successor.' The 'right successor' in this provision includes a person who succeeds to the claim by way of claim assignment. Where a transferee who has lawfully acquired a claim from a financial asset management company subsequently transfers the claim to another ordinary transferee, the enforcement court may, in accordance with the above provisions, rule to change the applicant for enforcement based on the claim assignment agreement and the application of the transferee or the transferor." Accordingly, this court directly treated the transferee in this case as the enforcement subject in the enforcement notice without making a ruling to change, which was procedurally improper. Therefore, on August 6, 2012, it issued Enforcement Ruling (2012) Min Zhi Yi Zi No. 1, revoking Enforcement Notice (2012) Min Zhi Xing Zi No. 8.

Li Xiaoling disagreed and applied for reconsideration to the Supreme People's Court, with the following main reasons: 1. Li Pengyu's status as a civil servant does not affect his eligibility as a transferee of the claim. 2. Before applying for enforcement, the two applicants had completed the claim assignment with 2234 Company and notified the debtor (i.e., the person subject to enforcement), making them lawful creditors. According to the relevant provisions of the Enforcement Provisions, as long as the applicant submits the effective legal instrument and the proof of succeeding to the right, etc., the applicant qualifies as an applicant for enforcement. This qualification was already reviewed at the case-filing stage, and the applicants were served with a notice of case acceptance. Reply No. 1 applies to situations where a change is applied for at the request of the transferee during the enforcement process. In this case, the applicants did not apply to change the enforcement subject during the enforcement process, so no ruling to change the applicant for enforcement was necessary.

Judgment: The Supreme People's Court issued Enforcement Ruling (2012) Zhi Fu Zi No. 26 on December 11, 2012, revoking the Enforcement Ruling (2012) Min Zhi Yi Zi No. 1 of the Fujian High Court, and ordering the Fujian High Court to re-issue enforcement notices to the two persons subject to enforcement.

Reasoning: The Supreme People's Court held that the disputed issues in this application for reconsideration were whether, when the rights holder confirmed by an effective legal instrument lawfully transfers its claim before entering into enforcement proceedings, the assignee of the claim, i.e., the right successor, may directly apply for enforcement as the applicant for enforcement, whether a ruling to change the applicant for enforcement is required, and how to handle disputes over the validity of the claim assignment contract during enforcement.

1. Regarding whether a ruling to change the applicant for enforcement is required. Changing the applicant for enforcement refers to changing a new rights holder to be the applicant for enforcement within an enforcement proceeding that has already begun based on the application of the original applicant for enforcement. According to Articles 18 and 20 of the Enforcement Provisions, a right successor has the right to apply for enforcement in its own name. As long as it submits to the People's Court the documents proving its succession to the right and proves that it is the right successor confirmed by the effective legal instrument, it meets the conditions for accepting an enforcement case. This situation is not a change of applicant for enforcement in the strict sense, but because the legal basis is the same, it can also be understood as a change of applicant for enforcement in a broad sense, i.e., resolving the issue of subject change at the case-filing stage. The opinion of Reply No. 1 is that Article 18 of the Enforcement Provisions can serve as the legal basis for changing the applicant for enforcement, and that the assignee of a claim can be regarded as the right successor under that provision. In this case, the original rights holder, 2234 Company, confirmed by the effective judgment, had already transferred the claim before enforcement began and did not participate in the enforcement proceedings as the applicant for enforcement. Instead, the right successors, Li Xiaoling and Li Pengyu, directly applied for enforcement under Article 18 of the Enforcement Provisions. Because their application had been accepted by the court for case filing, and the acceptance was by issuing a notice of acceptance rather than by a ruling, the assignees became the applicants for enforcement. Therefore, there was no need for the enforcement court to make a separate ruling to change the subject and then issue an enforcement notice; it should directly issue an enforcement notice. In practice, some courts in this situation first list the original rights holder as the applicant for enforcement and then, after enforcement begins, make a ruling to change the subject. Because this merely increases the workload without any substantive impact, it is not considered a procedural flaw. However, one cannot conversely conclude that the failure to make a subject-change ruling is a procedural error.

2. Regarding the dispute over the validity of the claim assignment contract, in principle, it should be resolved by filing a separate lawsuit. The enforcement procedure is not the appropriate procedure for reviewing, adjudicating, and resolving that issue. Paragraph 5 of the Minutes, which the person subject to enforcement invoked to argue that the transfer contract was invalid, also provides: In a lawsuit where the transferee asserts the claim against the debtor, if the debtor raises a defense that the non-performing claim transfer contract is invalid, the People's Court shall inform the debtor to file a separate lawsuit on the invalidity of the non-performing claim transfer contract with the same People's Court; if the debtor does not file a separate lawsuit, the People's Court shall not uphold the defense. As for the issue of Li Pengyu's qualification as an applicant for enforcement, because it was found during the review of the objection in this case that Li Pengyu clearly stated that he had withdrawn from the claim assignment and would no longer participate in the enforcement of this case, Li Pengyu should no longer be listed as an applicant for enforcement in the subsequent enforcement. However, absent other factors, this fact does not affect the assignment and enforcement qualification of the other assignee, Li Xiaoling. If Li Xiaoling requests to continue enforcement, the Fujian High Court shall continue enforcement with Li Xiaoling as the applicant for enforcement.

Guiding Case No. 35

Guangdong Longzheng Investment Development Co., Ltd. v. Guangdong Jingmao Auction Co., Ltd. — entrusted auction enforcement reconsideration case

(Adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on December 18, 2014)

Keywords: civil litigation; enforcement reconsideration; entrusted auction; malicious collusion; auction annulment

Ruling Gist: Where an auction house and a buyer are related, and the auction conduct exhibits the following circumstances, harming the lawful rights and interests of rights holders related to the subject matter, the People's Court may deem that the auction house and the buyer acted in malicious collusion and lawfully rule that the auction is void: (1) During the auction process, there were no other unrelated bidders participating in the bidding, or although there were other bidders participating, there was no full competitive bidding; (2) The appraised value of the auction subject matter is clearly lower than the actual price, yet the transaction is still concluded at that appraised value.

Relevant Legal Provisions: Article 58 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC; Article 65 of the Auction Law of the PRC

Basic Facts: In a case of illegal lending dispute between Guangzhou Baiyun Lifa Industrial Company (hereinafter referred to as Lifa Company) and Guangzhou Guangfeng Real Estate Construction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Guangfeng Company), Guangzhou Yinfeng Real Estate Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yinfeng Company), and Guangzhou Jinhui Real Estate Construction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jinhui Company), the Guangdong High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as Guangdong High Court) rendered Civil Judgment (1996) Yue Fa Jing Yi Chu Zi No. 4 on May 20, 1997, ordering Guangfeng Company and Yinfeng Company to jointly repay Lifa Company a loan of RMB 160,647,776.07 plus interest, and Jinhui Company to bear joint and several compensation liability.

During the enforcement of the aforementioned judgment, the Guangdong High Court ruled on February 11, 1998 to seal up the unsold portion of Guangfeng Building under the name of Guangfeng Company, with an area of 18,851.86 square meters. The next day, it entrusted Guangdong Jingmao Auction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jingmao Auction) for auction. In June of the same year, the Guangdong Yuecai Real Estate Appraisal Institute entrusted by the court issued an appraisal report concluding that the auction price of that portion of Guangfeng Building on June 12, 1998 was RMB 102,493,594. The case was later suspended for some reason.

In early 2001, the Guangdong High Court restarted the disposal procedure and on April 4 of the same year entrusted Jingmao Auction to auction the entire Guangfeng Building. In early November of the same year, the Guangdong High Court published an announcement in newspapers regarding the intended auction of the entire Guangfeng Building, requiring all rights holders or property buyers involved in Guangfeng Building to declare their rights and register with Jingmao Auction by November 30, 2001, pending handling by the Guangdong High Court. According to the announcement, the rights declared to Jingmao Auction included requests for delivery of presold units of Guangfeng Building, resettlement units, and requests for refund of purchase payments, construction funds, bank loans, etc., amounting to over RMB 1.5 billion, of which the purchase payments paid by buyers exceeded RMB 200 million.

On August 26, 2003, the Guangdong High Court entrusted Guangdong Caixing Asset Appraisal Co., Ltd. (formerly the Guangdong Yuecai Real Estate Appraisal Institute) to appraise the entire Guangfeng Building. On September 10 of the same year, the institute issued an appraisal report concluding that the market value of the entire Guangfeng Building (land area 3,009 square meters, building area 34,840 square meters) was RMB 34.45 million, and recommended that the auction reserve price be 70% of the market value, i.e., RMB 24.12 million. On October 17 of the same year, Jingmao Auction sold the entire Guangfeng Building to Guangdong Longzheng Investment Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Longzheng Company) for RMB 24.12 million. The Guangdong High Court issued Civil Ruling (1997) Yue Gao Fa Zhi Zi No. 7 on October 28 of the same year, confirming the transfer of the entire Guangfeng Building to Longzheng Company for RMB 24.12 million. On January 5, 2004, the court issued a notice of assistance in enforcement to the municipal land and housing authorities of Guangzhou, requesting the transfer of the entire property title of Guangfeng Building to the buyer, Longzheng Company, and stating that the rights of all original rights holders of Guangfeng Building, including buyers, transferees, mortgagees, persons to be relocated, or relocated households, would be handled by the court in accordance with the law. After acquiring Guangfeng Building, Longzheng Company continued to invest funds to complete the construction on the basis of the original main frame structure. After completion, it was renamed "Times International Building."

On June 2, 2011, after re-examining the case based on opinions from relevant departments, the Guangdong High Court issued Enforcement Ruling (1997) Yue Gao Fa Zhi Zi No. 7-1, finding that the shareholders of Jingmao Auction and the buyer Longzheng Company were relatives and had an affiliated relationship. The difference in the two appraised prices of Guangfeng Building was huge. The first appraisal covered approximately half of the building area of Guangfeng Building, while the second appraisal covered the entire building, but the second appraisal price was only 35% of the first appraisal price. Even considering market changes, the price change was clearly abnormal. According to Jingmao Auction's report, there were three bidders participating in the auction, but the other two bidders did not raise their paddles to bid. Longzheng Company thus succeeded in bidding with one raise at the starting price of RMB 24.12 million. However, after the court coordinated with relevant judicial authorities, the two persons could not be located. The court later issued a written notice to Jingmao Auction to provide the bidding materials of the two persons, but Jingmao Auction failed to provide them as required. Moreover, Jingmao Auction did not file with the administrative department for industry and commerce in accordance with the provisions of Article 4 of the Interim Measures for the Supervision and Administration of Auctions, which states: "An auction enterprise holding an auction activity shall file with the administrative department for industry and commerce at the location of the auction activity within seven days prior to the auction date... The auction enterprise shall, within 7 days after the conclusion of the auction activity, send the list of bidders and copies of their identification documents to the administrative department for industry and commerce at the location of the auction activity for filing." The existing evidence cannot confirm that the other two bidders participated in the auction. In summary, it can be determined that the auctioneer, Jingmao Auction, and the bidder, Longzheng Company, engaged in malicious collusion in the auction of Guangfeng Building, resulting in an unfair competitive bidding for Guangfeng Building and harming the interests of the buyers and other creditors. Pursuant to Article 58 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC (hereinafter referred to as the General Principles of the Civil Law) and Article 65 of the Auction Law of the PRC (hereinafter referred to as the Auction Law), the court ruled the auction void and revoked its Civil Ruling (1997) Yue Gao Fa Zhi Zi No. 7 issued on October 28, 2003. In response, the buyer, Longzheng Company, and Jingmao Auction respectively raised objections to the Guangdong High Court.

Longzheng Company and Jingmao Auction House, after their objections were rejected, applied to the Supreme People's Court for reconsideration. The main grounds for reconsideration were as follows: there were reasonable explanations for the significant difference between the two valuations of Guangfeng Building before and after; the valuation results were unrelated to the auction house and the buyer; the reserve price was also determined based on the actual circumstances at the time, and the auction transaction price was caused by objective market factors at the time; Jingmao Auction House's inability to provide information on the other two bidders did not violate Article 54, Paragraph 2 of the Auction Law, which stipulates that "the retention period for auction materials shall be calculated from the date of termination of the entrustment auction contract and shall not be less than five years"; the auction process for Guangfeng Building was open and lawful, with auction announcements published in newspapers four times before the auction, and the law did not prohibit companies with relatives of auction house shareholders from participating in the bidding. Therefore, there was no fact of malicious collusion between the auction house and the buyer that harmed the interests of property purchasers and other creditors, and the Guangdong High Court's presumption of malicious collusion between the bidder and the auction house was erroneous.

Judgment

The Guangdong High Court rendered Enforcement Ruling (2011) Yue Gao Fa Zhi Yi Zi No. 1 on October 9, 2011, upholding the opinion of Enforcement Ruling (1997) Yue Gao Fa Zhi Zi No. 7-1 and rejecting the objection. After the ruling was served, Longzheng Company and Jingmao Auction House applied to the Supreme People's Court for reconsideration. The Supreme People's Court rendered Enforcement Ruling (2012) Zhi Fu Zi No. 6 on June 15, 2012, rejecting the reconsideration requests of Longzheng Company and Jingmao Auction House.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held that: Auctions conducted upon entrustment by a people's court are judicial compulsory auctions, which differ from auctions conducted by citizens, legal persons, or other organizations upon their own entrustment to auction institutions. The people's court has the authority to review the legality of the auction procedure and auction results. Therefore, even if the auction has been concluded, if the people's court discovers that the entrusted auction conduct is unlawful, it may still, in accordance with Article 58 of the General Principles of the Civil Law, Article 65 of the Auction Law, and other legal provisions, rule that the auction is invalid if there is malicious collusion during the auction process that prevents fair bidding and harms the lawful rights and interests of others.

Whether there is malicious collusion between the buyer and the auction institution during the auction process should be comprehensively examined based on the auction process, auction results, and other aspects. If there is a connected relationship between the buyer and the auction institution, the auction process lacks sufficient competitive bidding, and the buyer and auction institution, knowing that the appraised value and transaction price of the subject matter are obviously too low, still transact at that low price, harming the lawful rights and interests of the parties concerned with the subject matter, it can be determined that there is malicious collusion between the two parties.

In this case, under the circumstances where there was a connected relationship between Jingmao Auction House and the buyer due to the kinship of shareholders, unless it can be proven that other unrelated bidders participated in the auction process and that there was sufficient competitive bidding, it can be presumed that there was collusion between Jingmao Auction House and the buyer. The burden of proof for sufficient competitive bidding shall be borne by Jingmao Auction House and the buyer with whom it is connected. After the auction concluded in 2003, in the auction report submitted by Jingmao Auction House to the Guangdong High Court, it stated that there were two other natural persons participating in the bidding, but they did not raise paddles for bidding during the on-site auction. The auction had only one bid and was concluded at the reserve price, with no competitive bidding. However, the buyer Longzheng Company and Jingmao Auction House could not provide information on the other two bidders. Upon review, the materials filed with the industry and commerce administrative authorities provided during reconsideration did not contain any information on the participation of the other two bidders. The fact that the auction materials had passed the retention period was not a valid reason for failing to provide information on the bidders. Accordingly, it cannot be determined that other bidders participated in the auction, and it can be determined that there was collusion between Jingmao Auction House and the buyer Longzheng Company.

Given that the auction in this case was concluded directly at a reserve price of 70% of the market value determined by the appraisal institution, whether the appraised value was reasonable directly affected whether the auction result was fair and reasonable. Previously, the appraised value for half of the property had exceeded RMB 100 million, but the appraised value for the entire property this time was only 35% of the appraised value for half of the property previously. The auction house, knowing the price was too low, arranged for relatives to purchase the property through a single round of bidding without multiple rounds, seriously infringing on the interests of others. The price difference between the auction of the entire building and the appraisal of part of the property was enormous, and the explanations of the auction house and the buyer were unconvincing, leading to a determination that there was malicious collusion between them. At the same time, the rights related to Guangfeng Building included applications for delivery of pre-sold units and resettlement units of Guangfeng Building, and applications for refund of purchase payments, project payments, bank loans, etc., totaling over RMB 1.5 billion. The registered purchase payments from property buyers alone exceeded RMB 200 million. However, the auction price in this case was only RMB 24.12 million, yielding no benefit to the enforcement applicant in this case, who had no priority right to receive payment, and was clearly a futile auction. Given that Jingmao Auction House was responsible for accepting declarations of rights related to Guangfeng Building and that the buyer was connected to it, it can be determined that Jingmao Auction House and the buyer were also aware of the above issues. Therefore, with respect to the infringement of the rights and interests of parties concerned with Guangfeng Building resulting from the auction in this case, Jingmao Auction House and the buyer Longzheng Company constituted malicious collusion.

In summary, the Guangdong High Court's determination that the auctioneer Jingmao Auction House and the buyer Longzheng Company had malicious collusion in the auction of Guangfeng Building, leading to the inability to conduct fair bidding in the auction of Guangfeng Building and harming the interests of property buyers and other creditors, was correct. Therefore, Enforcement Ruling (1997) Yue Gao Fa Zhi Zi No. 7-1 and Enforcement Ruling (2011) Yue Gao Fa Zhi Yi Zi No. 1 were not improper, and the grounds for reconsideration of Jingmao Auction House and Longzheng Company were untenable.

Guiding Case No. 36

Zhongtou Credit Guarantee Co., Ltd. v. Haitong Securities Co., Ltd., et al. — dispute over securities rights enforcement reconsideration

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on December 18, 2014)

Keywords: civil litigation; enforcement reconsideration; due creditor's right; assist in performance

Ruling Gist

If a judgment debtor, before receiving an enforcement notice from the enforcement court, has received a notice from another enforcement court requiring it to directly satisfy a creditor of the enforcement applicant with a debt confirmed by a legally effective judgment or ruling of a people's court, and has satisfied such debt, the enforcement court shall not include the portion of the debt already satisfied within the scope of enforcement.

Related Legal Provisions

Article 224, Paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC

Basic Facts

In the case of Zhongtou Credit Guarantee Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Zhongtou Company) v. Haitong Securities Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Haitong Securities), Haitong Securities Co., Ltd., Fuzhou Guangda Road Securities Business Department (hereinafter Haitong Securities Business Department), concerning a dispute over securities rights, the Fujian High People's Court (hereinafter Fujian High Court) rendered Civil Mediation Paper (2009) Min Min Chu Zi No. 3 on June 11, 2009, which became legally effective. Zhongtou Company applied for enforcement to the Fujian High Court on June 25, 2009. The Fujian High Court opened a case for enforcement on July 3 of the same year, and issued Enforcement Notice (2009) Min Zhi Xing Zi No. 99 to the judgment debtors, Haitong Securities Business Department and Haitong Securities, on July 15 of that month, ordering them to perform the obligations confirmed by the legal instrument.

The judgment debtors, Haitong Securities and Haitong Securities Business Department, objected to Enforcement Notice (2009) Min Zhi Xing Zi No. 99 of the Fujian High Court by filing a written objection with that court. The objection alleged that: on June 12, 2009, the judgment debtor had satisfied a due debt of RMB 11,222,761.55 owed to Zhongtou Company to Pan Ding, an enforcement creditor of Zhongtou Company, pursuant to a notice to satisfy a due creditor's right from the Beijing Dongcheng District People's Court (hereinafter Beijing Dongcheng Court), and remitted the amount into the account of Beijing Dongcheng Court; the Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate People's Court (hereinafter Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate Court), in order to enforce a dispute case between Shanghai Zhongwei Asset Management Co., Ltd. and Zhongtou Company, issued an assistance notice for enforcement to it and deducted RMB 8,777,238.45 from the bank deposit of Haitong Securities on June 22, 2009. A total of RMB 20 million had been paid to the creditors of Zhongtou Company, therefore, there was no fact of unperformed payment obligations confirmed by Civil Mediation Paper (2009) Min Min Chu Zi No. 3 between it and Zhongtou Company, and the enforcement notice issued by the Fujian High Court should be revoked. Accordingly, the Fujian High Court rendered Ruling (2009) Min Zhi Yi Zi No. 1, holding that the objection of the judgment debtor was established and revoking Enforcement Notice (2009) Min Zhi Xing Zi No. 99. The enforcement applicant, Zhongtou Company, dissatisfied, applied to the Supreme People's Court for reconsideration. The main grounds of the enforcement applicant were that: the notice to satisfy a due creditor's right from Beijing Dongcheng Court and the assistance notice for enforcement from Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate Court both violated the spirit of Reply No. (2000) Zhi Jian Zi No. 304 of the Supreme People's Court to the Jiangsu High People's Court, which stated that a debt confirmed by a court judgment is not subject to Article 300 of the Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC (hereinafter Article 300 of the Opinions), and the ruling of the Fujian High Court was erroneous.

Judgment

The Supreme People's Court rendered Enforcement Ruling (2010) Zhi Fu Zi No. 2 on April 13, 2010, rejecting the reconsideration request of Zhongtou Credit Guarantee Co., Ltd. and upholding Ruling (2009) Min Zhi Yi Zi No. 1 of the Fujian High Court.

Reasoning

The Supreme People's Court held that: Reply No. (2000) Zhi Jian Zi No. 304 of the Supreme People's Court was a response to an individual case and did not have general effect. With the adjustment of enforcement jurisdiction under the Civil Procedure Law, the view in that reply, which was based on the premise that enforcement could only be conducted by the court of first instance and thus held that a due creditor's right confirmed by a court judgment was not subject to Article 300 of the Opinions, was no longer reasonable. The correct interpretation of this issue should be: a creditor's right confirmed by a court judgment (or mediation paper, hereinafter collectively referred to as judgment) may also be enforced by a court other than the judgment court under the procedure set forth in Article 300 of the Opinions. Because the due creditor's right has already been confirmed by a court judgment, the third party (the judgment debtor's debtor) cannot raise an objection that the creditor's right does not exist (denying the conclusion of the effective judgment). In this case, Beijing Dongcheng Court and Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate Court were precisely enforcing the creditor's right confirmed by Civil Mediation Paper (2009) Min Min Chu Zi No. 3 of the Fujian High Court in accordance with the above spirit. The judgment debtor, Haitong Securities, had no right to raise an objection to the creditor's right confirmed by the effective mediation paper and could not resist the compulsory deduction by Shanghai No. 2 Intermediate Court. Its voluntary compliance with the notice from Beijing Dongcheng Court was also lawful.

The time at which the judgment debtors, Haitong Securities Business Department and Haitong Securities, received notices from the relevant courts and assisted the relevant courts in enforcement was before the Fujian High Court issued its enforcement notice to them. After they assisted the relevant courts with enforcement, the debt of RMB 20 million owed to the enforcement applicant, Zhongtou Company, under Civil Mediation Paper (2009) Min Min Chu Zi No. 3 was extinguished, and the judgment debtor was entitled to request that the Fujian High Court not enforce the mediation paper further.

In summary, Ruling (2009) Min Zhi Yi Zi No. 1 of the Fujian High Court had clear factual findings and correct application of law. Therefore, the reconsideration request of Zhongtou Company was rejected, and Ruling (2009) Min Zhi Yi Zi No. 1 of the Fujian High Court was upheld.

Guiding Case No. 37

Shanghai Jinwei Machinery Manufacturing Co., Ltd. v. Swiss Retech AG — enforcement reconsideration of an arbitration award

(Deliberated and adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Supreme People's Court, released on December 18, 2014)

Keywords: civil litigation; enforcement reconsideration; foreign-related arbitral award; enforcement jurisdiction; commencement of the limitation period for applying for enforcement

Ruling Gist

If a party applies to a people's court of China for enforcement of a legally effective foreign-related arbitral award and discovers that the person against whom enforcement is sought or its property is within the territory of China, the people's court of China shall have enforcement jurisdiction over the case. The limitation period for a party to apply to the court for compulsory enforcement shall run from the date the person against whom enforcement is sought or its property is discovered to be within the territory of China.

Related Legal Provisions

Articles 239 and 273 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC

Basic Facts

In the case of Shanghai Jinwei Machinery Manufacturing Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Jinwei Company) v. Swiss Retech AG (RETECH Aktiengesellschaft, hereinafter Retech Company), concerning a dispute over a sales contract, the China International Economic and Trade Arbitration Commission rendered an arbitral award on September 18, 2006. On August 27, 2007, Jinwei Company applied to the Lenzburg Court (hereinafter Lenzburg Court) in Switzerland for recognition and enforcement of the arbitral award, submitting a translation of the arbitral award translated by China Central Translation Agency and authenticated by the Shanghai Foreign Affairs Office and the Consulate General of Switzerland in Shanghai. On October 25 of the same year, the Lenzburg Court rejected Jinwei Company's application, finding that the translation of the arbitral award submitted by Jinwei Company did not satisfy the requirement under Article IV(2) of the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (hereinafter the New York Convention) that "the translation shall be certified by an official or sworn translator or by a diplomatic or consular agent." Subsequently, Jinwei Company submitted to the Lenzburg Court on two further occasions a translation of the arbitral award translated by a local Swiss translation agency and a translation translated by Shanghai Shangwai Translation Company and authenticated by the Shanghai Foreign Affairs Office and the Consulate General of Switzerland in Shanghai, in order to apply for enforcement. However, the court rejected both applications on March 17, 2009, and August 31, 2010, respectively, on the grounds that the translations of the arbitral award did not strictly comply with Article IV(2) of the New York Convention.

On July 30, 2008, Jinwei Company discovered that Retech Company had a batch of machinery and equipment on exhibition in the Pudong New Area of Shanghai, and on that same day applied to the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court (hereinafter Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate Court) for enforcement. The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate Court opened a case for enforcement on the same day and sealed up and seized the machinery and equipment exhibited by Retech Company. Retech Company then raised an objection, arguing that Jinwei Company's application for enforcement had exceeded the time limit prescribed by the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC (hereinafter the Civil Procedure Law), and requested that the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate Court not accept the case, lift the seizure, and stay the enforcement.

Judgment

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered Civil Ruling (2008) Hu Yi Zhong Zhi Zi No. 640-1 on November 17, 2008, rejecting Retech Company's objection. After the ruling was served, Retech Company applied to the Shanghai High People's Court for enforcement reconsideration. The Shanghai High People's Court rendered Enforcement Ruling (2009) Hu Gao Zhi Fu Yi Zi No. 2 on December 20, 2011, rejecting the reconsideration application.

Reasoning

The effective judgment of the court held that: The issues in dispute in this case were whether the people's court of China had jurisdiction over the case and from which date the limitation period for applying for enforcement should begin to run.

I. Concerning the issue of the enforcement jurisdiction of the Chinese court

Under the provisions of the Civil Procedure Law, if, in the case of an arbitral award rendered by a Chinese foreign-related arbitration institution, the person against whom enforcement is sought or its property is not within the territory of the PRC, the parties shall directly apply to a foreign court with jurisdiction for recognition and enforcement. Given that at the time the arbitral award in this case became effective, the person against whom enforcement was sought, Retech Company, and its property were not within the territory of China, the people's court did not have enforcement jurisdiction over the case at the time the arbitral award became effective.

On July 30, 2008, Jinwei Company discovered that the person against whom enforcement was sought, Retech Company, had property on exhibition in Shanghai. At that time, the fact that the person against whom enforcement was sought, Retech Company, had property within the territory of the PRC gave rise to enforcement jurisdiction of the Chinese court over this case. The enforcement applicant, relying on the provision of the Civil Procedure Law that "if one party fails to perform an arbitral award, the other party may apply to the intermediate people's court at the place of domicile of the person against whom the application is made or at the place where the property is located for enforcement," and based on the fact that the person against whom enforcement was sought had failed to perform the obligations under the arbitral award, exercised its right to request civil compulsory enforcement and applied to the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate Court for enforcement. This met the requirements under the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC for a people's court to have jurisdiction over the enforcement of a foreign-related arbitral award, and the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate Court had jurisdiction over this enforcement application.

Considering that the principle underlying the New York Convention is that arbitral awards meeting the basic conditions stipulated in the Convention shall be recognized and enforced in any Contracting State. The purpose of the New York Convention is to facilitate the smooth enforcement of arbitral awards in Contracting States, and it does not prohibit a party from applying for recognition and enforcement of the relevant arbitral award in multiple Convention States. The party against whom enforcement is sought may defend by proving that the obligations under the arbitral award have been performed, submitting to the court at the place of enforcement evidence of the amount of debt already satisfied, thereby preventing the person against whom enforcement is sought from being forced to perform repeatedly or beyond the scope of the award. Therefore, the exercise of enforcement jurisdiction by the people's court over this case was consistent with the spirit of the New York Convention and would not result in the person against whom enforcement is sought being forced to perform the obligations under the effective arbitral award repeatedly.

II. Concerning the issue of the commencement of the limitation period for applying for enforcement in this case

Under Article 215 of the Civil Procedure Law (as amended in 2007), "the limitation period for applying for enforcement shall be two years." "The limitation period provided in the preceding paragraph shall run from the last day of the performance period specified in the legal instrument; if a legal instrument provides for performance in installments, it shall run from the last day of each specified installment period; if a legal instrument does not specify a performance period, it shall run from the date the legal instrument takes effect." Given that the provisions of Chinese law regarding the commencement of the limitation period for applying for enforcement are made with respect to the general situation where, at the time a legal instrument takes effect, the person against whom enforcement is sought or its property is within the territory of China; whereas the specific circumstances of this case are that, at the time the arbitral award became effective, the Chinese court did not have enforcement jurisdiction over the case, and the party applied to a foreign court for recognition and enforcement of the award in accordance with the law but failed to obtain enforcement, and there was no issue of failing to exercise the right to apply for enforcement; the person against whom enforcement is sought had persistently refused to perform the legal obligations confirmed by the award; and the enforcement applicant applied to the people's court for enforcement immediately after discovering that the person against whom enforcement is sought had property within the territory of China. Considering that in such circumstances, there is significant uncertainty as to when a foreign person against whom enforcement is sought or its property will again enter the territory of China, the starting point of the limitation period for applying for enforcement should be reasonably determined in order to fairly protect the lawful rights and interests of the enforcement applicant.

When a creditor obtains an effective legal document with payment content, if the debtor fails to perform the obligations determined by the effective document, the creditor may apply to the court to exercise the power of compulsory enforcement to realize its substantive law claim. This right is the right to apply for civil compulsory enforcement. The existence of the right to apply for civil compulsory enforcement depends on the substantive right, its acquisition depends on the enforcement basis, and its exercise depends on enforcement jurisdiction. Enforcement jurisdiction is the foundation and prerequisite of the right to apply for civil compulsory enforcement. In judicial practice, the enforcement jurisdiction of the people's court and the party's right to apply for civil compulsory enforcement cannot be abstract or uncertain, but must be specific and operable.

When the obligor, Ruitai Ke Company, failed to perform the obligations determined by the arbitral award, the right holder, Jinwei Company, acquired the right to apply for civil compulsory enforcement. However, according to the provisions of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, for an application for enforcement of an arbitral award made by a foreign-related arbitration institution, if the party subject to enforcement or its property is not within the territory of the People's Republic of China, the party concerned shall directly apply to a foreign court with jurisdiction for recognition and enforcement. At this time, because the party subject to enforcement or its property was not within the territory of China, the Chinese court had no enforcement jurisdiction over the case. The applicant for enforcement, Jinwei Company, was not subjectively unwilling or negligent in exercising its rights, but rather, due to objective reasons, the dispute itself did not create a connecting point for the people's court's enforcement jurisdiction, resulting in its inability to apply to the people's court for enforcement.

After accepting an application for compulsory enforcement, the people's court shall examine whether the application was filed within the statutory limitation period. Having enforcement jurisdiction is a necessary prerequisite for the people's court to examine the relevant application of the applicant for enforcement. Therefore, the time limit for the applicant to apply for enforcement shall be calculated from the date on which enforcement jurisdiction is established, that is, the date on which the party subject to enforcement's executable property is discovered.
